chapter: San Francisco, the So Different Orchestra and Johnny
title: Purcell's Dance Hall and the So Different Orchestra on the Barbary Coast
summary: Spikes goes to San Francisco for the 1915 Fair, takes over the baritone chair at Purcell's and forms the So Different Orchestra.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: like that on it, and then we played the ragtime on the xylophones and things, and we played trumpets, then we played saxophones and then things like that, you know, and we had about twenty minutes of that, you know--five or six different instruments. And then I came home about '14, I think, and left my brother here, and I got tired of it, and he did a single for awhile with that, and when I came home in '14, why I worked around here six or seven months, then I went to 'Frisco for the Fair. And then I got to 'Frisco, and I got associated with some boys playing in Purcell's Dance Hall, which was one of the talks of the...which was one of the...uh, at that time, was talked about all over the world 'cause it was the Barbary Coast. You've heard so much about the great Barbary Coast. Well, all of the dance halls and all of the sailors and all the boats and everything would come in. Well, Purcell's was a big Negro place, and it was the hit of the street because it had the best entertainers and things in it. And we formed an orchestra called the So Different Orchestra because that was the name of his dance hall, and in that, they had...we had four or five girl entertainers and four or five men entertainers, and we played for all of them, and we stayed there for a couple of years, and...
That was what year you went up there?

The beginning of '15. See, the Fair started about April or May, and I went up about February or March. My brother Tom had a barber shop in...on this same street, about three or four doors from the dance hall, and he was a great friend of the man, Lester Mapp that owned the dance hall, and when I came up there,

why, there was a boy playing one of the greatest baritone players in the world named Roy...named Roy...but after awhile he "caught the Chinaman"--what they play lottery, they call it "Catching the Chinaman," and he won seven...eight hundred dollars, and he left. He bought him a taxi...er...a car and started a nickel taxi. What do you call it those days?
Uhh...yeah, I know what you mean.
You know, started his own little streetcar, like.
Jitney, of course. Yeah, and I got right in there and took his place, which was an awfully hard to follow, you know, 'cause he was one of the greatest in the world on that baritone.
